925.title: Practice in meetings
925.hook: listening, patience, and not needing to win
925.howItsDone: Quakers hold meetings for business in which decisions are reached without a vote, by seeking the sense of the meeting; Christians read James 1:19 as a rule for everyday speech.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the commute: Thoreau's saunterers, and the going out and the coming in. Your line was the road.

Someone is speaking. Around the table, or across a grid of small faces on a screen, people nod. Some are listening. Some are rehearsing the clever thing they'll say the moment there's a gap. One has the camera off and is answering email. The speaker finishes, and three people start talking at once. Nobody meant any harm. A meeting just has a way of turning into a contest without anyone deciding it should. Old texts about speech and silence speak to that room. Today: Quaker meeting.
screen: `SOMEONE IS SPEAKING.` → `REHEARSING THE REPLY.` → `A CONTEST NOBODY CHOSE.`

segments.voice: First, the letter of James, in the King James Bible: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." Hearing comes first, and it's the only one of the three meant to be quick. Speaking waits. Anger waits too. Second, Proverbs names the opposite: "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him." That's the reply that starts before the question is finished, ready because it was never really listening. Third, a tradition with a way of meeting. In a Quaker meeting for business, among the Religious Society of Friends, decisions are made without a vote. Friends speak, they listen, they sit in silence, and they seek what Friends call the sense of the meeting. It can be slow. It's built on the idea that the answer may come from anyone in the room, including someone quiet in the corner. Fourth, not needing to win. The Tao Te Ching, in its twenty-second chapter, says that because the sage does not strive, no one in the world can strive with him. In a meeting that looks plain: letting someone finish a sentence, asking a real question instead of making a point, letting a good idea be someone else's. Listening isn't agreeing. It's letting a person be fully heard before you answer. A simple test helps: before speaking, could you say back what the last person meant, in a way they'd recognize? If not, the turn to speak can wait one more breath.
screen: `SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.` · `ANSWERING BEFORE HEARING.` · `THE SENSE OF THE MEETING.` · `NO NEED TO WIN.` · then, large: `LISTEN IN THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Picture your next meeting, or a conversation at home that tends to turn into a contest, and the person who most often frustrates you there. Imagine letting them finish every sentence, and when the urge to prepare your reply comes, set it down the way you'd set down a cup. Then find one real question you could ask them instead of a point to make; if you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words.
Quaker meeting. Where Friends speak, listen, sit in silence, and seek what they call the sense of the meeting. Today's word.
Your line: listen in the room. The answer may come from the quiet one in the corner. Day nine hundred twenty-five, done.

926.title: Practice in messages
926.hook: write every message as if to a person, because it is
926.howItsDone: Buddhists practice right speech, one part of the Noble Eightfold Path; Jews and Christians turn to Proverbs, and Christians also to the letters of Paul, for guidance on how to speak, and some apply the same teachings to writing.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Quaker meeting: swift to hear, slow to speak, and seeking the sense of the meeting. Your line was listen in the room.

A message with no greeting and no name: need this today. It was typed in a hurry, between two other things, and sent without a second look. On the other end, someone reads it standing at a kitchen counter. Then reads it again. Are they in trouble? Is something wrong? There's no face to check, no tone of voice, just the words, and the reader fills in the rest. Behind the screen name there's a person with a morning of their own. Today: Colossae.
screen: `NEED THIS TODAY.` → `READ IT AGAIN.` → `BEHIND THE SCREEN NAME.`

segments.voice: First, Proverbs, in the King James Bible: "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger." Soft doesn't mean vague or weak. It means not grievous: not the word that wounds when a plainer one would do. Second, a letter of Paul's, to the Christians at Colossae: "Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man." Grace and salt together: kind, but with some flavor in it. Honest, not syrup. Third, the Buddha. In a short teaching in the Anguttara Nikaya, he names five marks of speech that is well spoken: it's spoken at the right time, it's true, it's gentle, it's beneficial, and it's spoken with a mind of goodwill. They fit a message almost too well. Is this the right time, or is it eleven at night? Is it true? Is it gentle? Does it help? Is it written with goodwill, or with a sigh? Fourth, why messages need this. Speech in a room comes with a face, a tone, a chance to fix a misunderstanding on the spot. A message arrives bare, and the reader supplies the tone, sometimes harsher than the writer meant. So the practice is small: write every message as if to a person, because it is. A greeting. A name. A thank you. A when you have a moment. One word can be the difference between a soft answer and a grievous one.
screen: `A SOFT ANSWER TURNETH AWAY WRATH.` · `GRACE, SEASONED WITH SALT.` · `FIVE MARKS OF GOOD SPEECH.` · `A MESSAGE ARRIVES BARE.` · then, large: `A PERSON READS IT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one message you need to send, or one you sent recently, and picture the person reading it: where they are, what kind of day they might be having. Read your words slowly, as they would, through the Buddha's five marks: the right time, true, gentle, helpful, written with goodwill. Find one word to change or add, a greeting, their name, a thank you; if you pray, you can hold that person in your own tradition's words.
Colossae. The city Paul wrote to, telling the Christians there to season their speech with grace, like salt. Today's word.
Your line: a person reads it. A message arrives bare, so the kindness has to travel in the words. Until tomorrow.

927.title: Work and home
927.hook: keep the people you work for in view
927.howItsDone: People who try to keep work and home in balance often set a fixed time to stop, close the laptop or leave the workplace at that hour, and protect certain evenings or meals for the people at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Colossae, where Paul told the Christians to season their speech with grace. Your line was a person reads it.

Two plates on a kitchen table, and one chair still empty. A child has a drawing ready to show someone. A dog sits by the door with its ears up. A friend has texted twice. None of them are in anyone's calendar, and none of them will send a reminder. Somewhere else, the person they're waiting for is answering one more email, fixing one more small thing. They just wait. The old question is who all this work is for. Today: Ecclesiastes.
screen: `TWO PLATES, ONE CHAIR EMPTY.` → `A DRAWING, A DOG, TWO TEXTS.` → `WHO IS THIS FOR?`

segments.voice: First, a man with no end to his work. The book of Ecclesiastes describes him: alone, no child, no brother, and still no end of all his labor, his eye never satisfied with riches. The writer notes the one question he never asks, in the King James words: "For whom do I labour, and bereave my soul of good?" The writer calls it vanity, and a sore travail. Second, the turn. For some people, the honest answer to that question is a short list of names. The rent paid, the groceries bought, the school shoes, the trip to see a grandmother. The work was for them all along. But work has a way of quietly swapping places with the people it was meant to serve. The job grows to fill the evening, and the ones it was for get what's left. Third, the psalm. Psalm 127 says it plainly: "It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep." Readers take that line in different ways. Some hear trust in God, who builds the house. Some hear permission to rest. Either way, the psalm doesn't praise the late night. Fourth, the practice of leaving. Leaving on time is a small act, and it says something. To the people at home: you are the reason, not the leftover. To the work: you matter, and you are not everything. Some days the work really can't wait, and that's honest too. But if it never waits, the people do. And people who wait long enough sometimes stop waiting.
screen: `NO END OF ALL HIS LABOR.` · `THE WORK WAS FOR THEM.` · `SO HE GIVETH HIS BELOVED SLEEP.` · `LEAVING ON TIME SAYS SOMETHING.` · then, large: `FOR WHOM?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people your work is for, not the clients or the boss, but a partner, a child, a parent, a friend, even yourself. Picture one of them at the moment you usually arrive late. Then picture closing the laptop at a set hour and walking in while they're still waiting; if you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words.
Ecclesiastes. Whose Preacher asks the question some never do: for whom do I labor, and deprive myself of good? Today's word.
Your line: they're waiting. The work was for them all along. That's day nine hundred twenty-seven.

928.title: Stages of life
928.hook: Hindu tradition names four stages of life, from student to renunciant
928.howItsDone: Hindus who follow the ashrama pattern treat each stage as having its own duties: study for the student, work and family for the householder, a gradual stepping back for the forest dweller, and renunciation for those who take sannyasa.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Ecclesiastes, and its question: for whom do I labor? Your line was they're waiting.

A student cramming for exams wants to know why nobody will let her just get on with her life. A parent can't remember the last time the house was quiet. A man, newly retired, stands in the kitchen at ten in the morning and has no idea what he's for. Each of them is asking the same question at a different hour: what is this part of my life supposed to be about? Hindu tradition has an old answer. Not one rule for a whole life, but four. Today's word: ashrama.
screen: `A STUDENT, A PARENT, A RETIREE.` → `WHAT IS THIS PART FOR?` → `FOUR STAGES.`

segments.voice: First, the four. In Hindu tradition, the ashramas are stages of life. In the student stage, brahmacharya, a young person learns from a teacher. In the householder stage, grihastha, a person marries, works, raises a family and keeps a home. In the forest stage, vanaprastha, the forest dweller steps back from the busy middle of life. And in sannyasa, the renunciant lets go of home and possessions altogether. Second, the hinge. The Laws of Manu, an old Hindu law book, gives a picture of when to move on. In paraphrase: when a householder sees his skin wrinkled, his hair white, and the sons of his sons, he may go to the forest. Not a birthday. The sign is that the next generation has arrived. Third, the householder's honor. It's easy to hear the stages as a ladder, with the renunciant at the top and the busy parent at the bottom. Manu says something different about the middle. As all creatures live by the air, the other stages live by the householder's support. The student is fed, the wanderer is given alms, because someone is working and keeping a home. In this picture, work isn't a detour from the spiritual life. For a season, it is the spiritual life. Fourth, a map, not a cage. The old texts were written for men of particular classes, and Hindus read and live the stages in different ways today, some as a strict pattern, some as a loose map. What the map offers anyone is a question: not what is life for, but what is this stage for?
screen: `STUDENT, HOUSEHOLDER, FOREST, RENUNCIANT.` · `GRAY HAIR AND GRANDCHILDREN.` · `ALL LIVE BY THE HOUSEHOLDER.` · `A MAP, NOT A CAGE.` · then, large: `ASHRAMA.`

segments.voice: Hear the four names again, student, householder, forest dweller, renunciant, and without judging, ask which one describes this season of your life; maybe more than one. Name your stage quietly to yourself. Then ask what this stage asks of you, not forever, just now, and stay with the first plain answer.
Ashrama. A stage of life in Hindu tradition: student, householder, forest dweller, renunciant, each with its own work. Today's word.

929.title: Play is work
929.hook: play is children's work, and adults need it too
929.howItsDone: Adults who make room for play often set aside short, regular times for games, music, sport, drawing or play with children, and treat that time as protected rather than as a reward for finishing work.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ashrama: student, householder, forest dweller, renunciant, each stage with its own work. Your line was my stage.

A small girl is building a tower of blocks on the kitchen floor. Her face is fierce. Her tongue is out. When it falls, she doesn't laugh it off; she starts again, more carefully, at the base. Call her to dinner and she'll tell you, quite seriously, that she's busy. She is. There's a saying, sometimes credited to the educator Maria Montessori: play is the work of the child. Somewhere between that kitchen floor and the office, the habit can get lost. Today: lila.
screen: `A TOWER OF BLOCKS.` → `SHE'S BUSY.` → `PLAY IS THE WORK OF THE CHILD.`

segments.voice: First, the child's side. Watch a child at play and you see what this path has been calling work: absorption, practice, trying again after failure, learning the shape of the world with the hands. Whoever first said play is a child's work, the point stands. It isn't a break from growing up. It's how growing up happens. Second, a city full of play. When the prophet Zechariah describes a Jerusalem restored and at peace, one picture he gives is this: "And the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing in the streets thereof." Old men and old women live in those streets again, each with a staff in hand, the verse before says, and children play. Peace, in that picture, looks like a game in the street. Third, the world as play. In Hindu thought there's a word, lila, which means play. The Brahma Sutras, an ancient Hindu text, ask a hard question: why would a God who lacks nothing create a world at all? The answer, in paraphrase: like the play of someone who already has everything, not for need, simply for play. Some Hindu traditions see the whole world as divine play. Fourth, the adult's side. Grown-ups easily treat play as a reward for finishing the real work, and the real work never finishes. But play does things work can't. It has no outcome to protect. You can lose and nothing breaks. For ten minutes, the watching, measuring part of us gets time off. That isn't laziness. In the small builder's words, it's being busy.
screen: `HOW GROWING UP HAPPENS.` · `BOYS AND GIRLS PLAYING IN THE STREETS.` · `LILA: THE WORLD AS PLAY.` · `NOTHING BREAKS WHEN YOU LOSE.` · then, large: `PLAY IS WORK.`

segments.voice: Go back to a game you loved as a child, hide and seek, a ball against a wall, drawing, a made-up world in the yard, and remember where you played it, and who with. Notice whatever comes, without telling yourself what it should be. Then let one small kind of play come to mind, a puzzle, a song, a silly drawing, something with no point except itself.
Lila. The Hindu word for play: some traditions see the whole world as divine play, not born of need. Today's word.
Your line: play. If someone calls you away from it, you're allowed to say you're busy. Day nine hundred twenty-nine, done.

930.title: May Day
930.hook: many countries honor workers on 1 May or in early September
930.howItsDone: On workers' days, people take part in parades and gatherings, take a day off, or simply rest; some Catholics keep 1 May as the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was lila, play, and Zechariah's city with streets full of children playing. Your line was play.

A cup of morning coffee passes through more hands than anyone drinking it will ever meet. Someone picked the beans. Someone drove the truck. Someone stocked the shelf, someone fixed the pipe that brings the water, someone cleaned the floor of the shop before it opened. Their faces aren't on the cup, and their names aren't on the receipt. In a number of countries, one day a year tries to fix that. In some it falls on the first of May. In the United States and Canada, it's Labor Day, in early September. Today: May Day.
screen: `MORE HANDS THAN YOU'LL MEET.` → `NO NAMES ON THE CUP.` → `A DAY FOR THE WORKERS.`

segments.voice: First, the day itself. Workers' days are marked in different ways: parades, speeches, a day off, a cookout at the end of summer. Some are political, some just restful. The idea underneath is simple: the people who do the work should be seen. Second, an old law about wages. The book of Leviticus sets a rule about hired workers. In the King James words: "the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning." Pay the day laborer the same day. Deuteronomy explains why: he is poor, and he has set his heart on it. A day's wage held back overnight is a family's dinner held back. Third, a teaching in Islam. A hadith, a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, reported in Ibn Majah, says, in paraphrase: give the worker his wages before his sweat dries. Not next month. Not after the paperwork. Two traditions, the same urgency about the person who did the work. Fourth, a saint in an apron. The Catholic Church keeps the first of May as a feast of Saint Joseph the Worker, the carpenter of Nazareth. So on the same day some streets fill with banners, some churches remember a man with sawdust on his sleeves. What these share is a turn of attention. The finished thing, the coffee, the clean floor, the working pipe, is easy to see. The hands that made it are easy to miss. A workers' day is a day for looking past the thing to the hands.
screen: `THE PEOPLE WHO WORK, SEEN.` · `PAY BEFORE THE MORNING.` · `BEFORE HIS SWEAT DRIES.` · `SAINT JOSEPH THE WORKER.` · then, large: `MAY DAY.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind one ordinary thing you've used today, a cup, a light switch, a bus seat, and trace it backward one pair of hands at a time: who made it, who moved it, who kept it working, who cleaned up after. You won't know their names; just let them be there, one after another. If you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words.
May Day. A day for honoring workers, kept on the first of May in some countries and in early September in others. Today's word.
Your line: thank the workers. Every finished thing has hands behind it. That's day nine hundred thirty.

931.title: Sukkot, the booth
931.hook: at harvest, Jews live in booths open to the sky (Leviticus 23:42)
931.howItsDone: During Sukkot, Jewish families build a sukkah, a hut roofed with branches, and eat meals in it, with some sleeping there too; guests are welcomed into the booth.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was May Day: pay before the morning, and before the sweat dries. Your line was thank the workers.

In a backyard, on a balcony, in a parking lot behind a synagogue, someone is building a hut. Four walls, more or less. A roof of branches and leaves, laid loose on purpose, so the stars can show through. Paper chains, a folding table, a wobbly chair. For a week, the family will eat here, sit here, and some will sleep here, while their solid house stands empty a few steps away. The harvest is in. The barns are full. And this is where they choose to live. Today: Sukkot.
screen: `A HUT IN THE BACKYARD.` → `A ROOF YOU CAN SEE THROUGH.` → `THE HOUSE STANDS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: First, the command. Sukkot means booths, and the festival comes straight from the book of Leviticus. In the King James words: "Ye shall dwell in booths seven days." The next verse gives the reason: so that each generation knows that God made the children of Israel dwell in booths when they came out of Egypt. Second, the roof. The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish law, works out what makes a booth count. In paraphrase: if the sunlight inside is more than the shade, it isn't a proper sukkah. So the roof has to give real shade, yet stay loose, made of things that grew from the ground. Shelter, but not a fortress. Third, the timing. This is a harvest festival. You'd expect the moment the grain is safely stored to be the moment you settle into your strongest house. Instead, the Torah sends people out under a fragile roof, at the very moment of plenty. Some read it as a reminder that the full barn isn't what keeps you safe. Fourth, the joy. Deuteronomy says of this feast, "And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast," and lists who rejoices: sons and daughters, servants, the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow. The booth isn't for the family alone. It's a table with room for whoever is outside. A fitting end to this week of listening in meetings, softening messages, leaving work on time, naming a stage of life, play, and thanking the workers. Sukkot adds one more: when the work is done, step out from behind the walls and make room.
screen: `YE SHALL DWELL IN BOOTHS.` · `MORE SHADE THAN SUN.` · `A FRAGILE ROOF AT HARVEST.` · `ROOM FOR THE STRANGER.` · then, large: `SUKKOT.`

segments.voice: Notice what's over your head right now: a ceiling, a sky, branches, clouds. Picture a roof of leaves with light coming through the gaps, and ask yourself what keeps you safe, really. Then let one meal under the sky come to mind, and who might share it; if you pray, you can hold that table in your own tradition's words.
Sukkot. Booths. The Jewish harvest festival when families live in huts open to the sky, with room for the stranger. Today's word.
Your line: the booth. A fragile roof, and room at the table for the stranger. See you tomorrow.
